summary: Describes extensions that let iSCSI run over an RDMA-capable protocol such as iWARP, so data can move directly into SCSI buffers without extra copies. It was replaced by RFC 7145.

plainLanguage.summary: iSCSI sends storage commands over TCP, and TCP has to put arriving data in order before it can be used. This RFC defines iSER, which runs iSCSI over a transport that can move data straight into the right memory, so the copy and the wait both go away.

subtitle: How iSCSI storage traffic can run over RDMA so data lands directly in the right memory buffers.

tldr.problem: iSCSI runs over TCP, so data that arrives out of order has to be buffered and reassembled before it can be placed into the iSCSI buffers. At high speeds that copying wastes memory bandwidth and processor cycles and adds delay.
tldr.mechanism: iSER maps iSCSI messages onto the remote direct memory access operations of an RDMA-capable transport such as iWARP. The initiator advertises a buffer with a steering tag, and the target then reads that buffer or writes into it directly, so the data never has to be copied into an intermediate buffer.
tldr.outcome: RFC 5046 was a Proposed Standard. It has been obsoleted by RFC 7145 and updated by RFC 7146.

sections.title: Why iSCSI Needs RDMA
sections.content:
The iSCSI protocol is a mapping of the SCSI Architecture Model over the TCP protocol. SCSI commands are carried by iSCSI requests, and SCSI responses and status are carried by iSCSI responses. Other iSCSI protocol exchanges and SCSI data are also transported in iSCSI protocol data units.

Out-of-order TCP segments in the traditional iSCSI model have to be stored and reassembled before the iSCSI protocol layer within an end node can place the data in the iSCSI buffers. The reassembly is required because not every TCP segment is likely to contain an iSCSI header to enable its placement, and TCP itself does not have a built-in mechanism for signalling upper layer protocol message boundaries to aid placement of out-of-order segments.

The RFC lists what that costs at high network speeds: wasted memory bandwidth in data copying, the need for reassembly memory, wasted processor cycles in data copying, and the general store-and-forward delay from an application's point of view.

TCP reassembly was already recognised as a serious issue in RFC 3720, where the notion of a sync and steering layer was introduced as optional to implement and use. One specific mechanism, called markers, was defined there, providing an application-level way of framing iSCSI protocol data units within the TCP data stream even when the TCP segments are not yet reassembled into order. With those techniques a network interface controller customised for iSCSI could offload the TCP and IP processing and support direct data placement, but most iSCSI implementations do not support iSCSI markers, which makes marker-based direct data placement unusable in practice.

The iWARP protocol stack provides direct data placement that is usable in practice, and there is interest in using iSCSI with other remote direct memory access stacks that support it, such as the one provided by InfiniBand. The generic term RDMA-Capable Protocol is used for the remote direct memory access functionality provided by such stacks.

iSER's goal is to let iSCSI employ direct data placement and RDMA capabilities using a generic RDMA-capable controller, so that the stack scales to high speeds by relying on a generic data placement process and on products that place both in-order and out-of-order data directly. The document describes iSER as a protocol extension to iSCSI, both for convenience of description and because it is true in a strict protocol sense, but notes that iSER is in reality extending the connectivity of the iSCSI protocol defined in RFC 3720. Where plain iSCSI is meant, the RFC uses the term Traditional iSCSI.
sections.plainLanguage: TCP promises to deliver bytes in order, so a receiver has to hold the pieces that arrive early until the missing ones show up. For storage traffic that means a copy into a holding area and then a copy out again.

sections.title: The Layering
sections.content:
iSER is layered between the iSCSI layer and the RDMA-capable protocol layer. The RDMA-capable layer may be composed of one or more distinct protocol layers, depending on the specifics of that protocol. For TCP the RDMA-capable protocol is iWARP; for InfiniBand it is the Reliable Connected Transport Service.

The document lists the architectural goals that shaped the design. They are to provide an RDMA data transfer model for iSCSI that enables direct in-order or out-of-order placement of SCSI data into pre-allocated SCSI buffers while maintaining in-order data delivery; not to require any major changes to the SCSI Architecture Model or to SCSI command set standards; to use existing iSCSI infrastructure, including the management information base, bootstrapping, negotiation, naming and discovery, and security; to require a session to operate in the traditional iSCSI data transfer mode if iSER is not supported by either the initiator or the target; to allow initiator and target implementations to use generic RDMA-capable controllers such as RDMA-enabled network interface controllers, or to implement iSCSI and iSER in software, without requiring iSCSI- or iSER-specific assists; to require full and only generic RDMA-capable functionality at both ends; and to implement a lightweight datamover protocol for iSCSI with minimal state maintenance.

The protocol overview then spells out the shape of the thing. iSER-assisted mode is negotiated during the iSCSI login for each session, and an entire iSCSI session can only operate in one mode. Once in iSER-assisted mode, all iSCSI interactions on that connection use RDMA-capable protocol messages. A Send message type carries an iSCSI control-type protocol data unit preceded by an iSER header, while RDMA Write, RDMA Read Request and RDMA Read Response messages carry the control and all data information associated with the iSCSI data-type protocol data units. The target drives all data transfer for SCSI writes and SCSI reads, with the exception of iSCSI unsolicited data, by issuing RDMA Read Requests and RDMA Writes respectively. The RDMA-capable protocol is responsible for ensuring data integrity, which is why iSCSI header and data digests are negotiated to None for iSCSI/iSER sessions. The iSCSI error recovery hierarchy is fully supported, and iSER requires no changes to iSCSI authentication, security and text mode negotiation mechanisms.
sections.plainLanguage: iSER sits between the storage protocol and the fast transport, and it does not change either of them. It only decides which memory operation each message becomes.

sections.title: The Four RDMA Services iSER Uses
sections.content:
A Steering Tag is the identifier of an I/O buffer, unique to an RDMA-capable controller, that the iSER layer advertises to the remote iSCSI/iSER node in order to complete a SCSI I/O. Advertisement is the act of informing the target by the initiator that an I/O buffer is available at the initiator for RDMA Read or RDMA Write access by the target. The initiator advertises the buffer by including the steering tag in the header of an iSER message containing the SCSI command protocol data unit. The base tagged offset is not explicitly specified, but the target must always assume it as zero, and the buffer length is as specified in the SCSI command protocol data unit.

The advertised steering tag is automatically invalidated upon a normal completion of the associated task, realised through the Send with Solicited Event and Invalidate message carrying the SCSI response protocol data unit. There are two exceptions: bidirectional commands, and abnormal completion of a command. In those cases the initiator is required to explicitly invalidate the tag, in addition to sanity checking the automatic invalidation.

Send is the RDMA operation that is not addressed to an advertised buffer by the sending side, and thus uses untagged buffers on the receiving side. The initiator uses Send to transmit any iSCSI control-type protocol data unit to the target, for example the SCSI command protocol data unit, and the target uses Send to transmit any iSCSI control-type protocol data unit to the initiator, for example the SCSI response protocol data unit.

RDMA Write is the operation used to place data into an advertised buffer on the receiving side; the sending side addresses the message using a steering tag and a tagged offset that are valid on the data sink. The target uses it to transfer the contents of a local I/O buffer to an advertised I/O buffer at the initiator, to transfer whole or part of the data required to complete a SCSI read command. The initiator does not employ RDMA Writes.

RDMA Read is the operation used to retrieve data from an advertised buffer on a remote node. The sending side of the RDMA Read Request addresses the message using a steering tag and a tagged offset valid on the data source, in addition to providing a valid local steering tag and tagged offset that identify the data sink. The target uses it to fetch whole or part of the data required to complete a SCSI write command. The initiator does not employ RDMA Reads.
sections.plainLanguage: Four operations cover everything: a tag that names a buffer, a way to send a message, a way to put data into a buffer, and a way to take data out of one.

sections.title: How a SCSI Read and Write Run
sections.content:
For a SCSI read, the iSER layer at the initiator receives the SCSI command protocol data unit from the iSCSI layer. It generates a steering tag for the I/O buffer of the SCSI read and advertises the buffer by including that tag as part of the iSER header for the protocol data unit. The iSER message is transferred to the target using a SendSE message. The iSER layer at the target then uses one or more RDMA Writes to transfer the data required to complete the SCSI read, placing it straight into the buffer the initiator advertised. Finally the target uses a SendInvSE message to transfer the SCSI response protocol data unit back to the initiator, and the initiator's iSER layer notifies the iSCSI layer of the availability of the response.

For a SCSI write, the initiator again receives the SCSI command protocol data unit and, if solicited data transfer is involved, generates a steering tag for the I/O buffer of the write and advertises the buffer in the iSER header of the SendSE message carrying the command. The initiator may optionally send one or more non-immediate unsolicited data protocol data units to the target using Send message types. If solicited data transfer is involved, the target uses one or more RDMA Reads to transfer the data required to complete the write, pulling it out of the initiator's advertised buffer. The target then sends the SCSI response back with a SendInvSE message, and the initiator notifies the iSCSI layer that the response is available.
sections.plainLanguage: For a read, the target pushes the data into a buffer the initiator offered. For a write, the target pulls the data out of one. Either way the bytes never pass through a buffer on the way.

sections.title: The iSER Header
sections.content:
An iSER header must be present in every Send message type of the RDMA-capable protocol. The header is located in the first 12 bytes of the message payload of the Send message type, and its layout is the one drawn in Figure 2 of the RFC: a four-bit Opcode field followed by opcode specific fields filling the rest of the header.

The Opcode field identifies the type of iSER message. The value 0001b means an iSCSI control-type protocol data unit, 0010b means an iSER Hello message and 0011b means an iSER HelloReply message. All other opcodes are reserved.

For an iSCSI control-type protocol data unit, the header also carries two validity flags and the two steering tags. The Write STag Valid flag is one bit and indicates whether the Write STag field of the header is valid; if set to zero the field must be ignored at the receiver. It is set to one when there is solicited data to be transferred for a SCSI write or bidirectional command, or when there are non-immediate unsolicited and solicited data to be transferred for the referenced task in a Task Management Function Request with the TASK REASSIGN function. The Read STag Valid flag is one bit with the same meaning for the Read STag field; it is set to one for a SCSI read or bidirectional command, or for a Task Management Function Request with the TASK REASSIGN function.

The Write STag field is 32 bits and holds the Write STag when the valid flag is set. For a SCSI write or bidirectional command it advertises the initiator's I/O buffer containing the solicited data, and it is used as the data source steering tag in the resulting RDMA Read operations. When the valid flag is zero the field must be set to zero. The Read STag field is 32 bits and holds the Read STag when its valid flag is set, advertising the initiator's read I/O buffer and used as the data sink steering tag in the resulting RDMA Write operations; it too must be set to zero when its flag is zero. Reserved fields must be set to zero on transmit and must be ignored on reception.
sections.plainLanguage: Every iSER message starts with a short header that says what kind of message it is and, when relevant, names the two buffers involved.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
When iSER is layered on top of an RDMA-capable protocol layer, the security considerations of iSER are the same as those of the underlying layer. For iWARP these are described in the RDMA protocol specification and in the direct data placement security document.

Since the iSER-assisted iSCSI protocol is still functionally iSCSI from a security considerations perspective, all of the iSCSI security requirements described in RFC 3720 and RFC 3723 apply. If the IPsec mechanism is used, it must be established before the connection transitions to iSER-assisted mode. If iSER is layered on top of a non-IP based RDMA-capable layer, all the security protocol mechanisms applicable to that layer are also applicable to an iSCSI/iSER connection. If iSER is layered on top of a non-IP protocol, the IPsec mechanism must be implemented at any point where the iSER protocol enters the IP network, for example via gateways, and the non-IP protocol should implement a packet-by-packet security protocol equal in strength to IPsec.

The final rule addresses denial of service. To minimize the potential for a denial-of-service attack, the iSCSI layer must not request that the iSER layer allocate the connection resources necessary to support the RDMA-capable protocol until the iSCSI layer is sufficiently far along in the iSCSI Login Phase that it is reasonably certain that the peer side is not an attacker.
sections.plainLanguage: iSER adds no security of its own: whatever protects the transport protects iSER, and the iSCSI rules still apply on top.
